topics.title: The preterite — what you did
topics.description: Talk about finished actions: 'I ate', 'we went', 'she said'.

guide.intro: The preterite (pretérito indefinido) is Spanish's main 'simple past' tense. You use it for actions that started and finished at a specific point — 'I called her yesterday', 'we ate at eight'.

sections.text: Drop the -ar/-er/-ir and add these endings. Notice the stress marks on the yo and él forms — they're load-bearing.

rows.source: hablar → hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablasteis, hablaron
rows.translation: I spoke, you spoke, he/she spoke, we spoke, you (pl.) spoke, they spoke

rows.source: comer → comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron
rows.translation: I ate, you ate, he/she ate, we ate, you (pl.) ate, they ate

rows.source: vivir → viví, viviste, vivió, vivimos, vivisteis, vivieron
rows.translation: I lived, you lived, he/she lived, we lived, you (pl.) lived, they lived

sections.text: Four verbs you'll use constantly have irregular preterites. Memorize them — they don't follow the rules.

rows.source: ser / ir → fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron
rows.translation: I was / I went (yes, same forms for both!)

rows.source: hacer → hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicisteis, hicieron
rows.translation: to do/make — 'hizo' has a z, not c

rows.source: decir → dije, dijiste, dijo, dijimos, dijisteis, dijeron
ver → vi, viste, vio, vimos, visteis, vieron
rows.translation: to see — no accents on 'vi' or 'vio'

sections.text: Time markers that scream 'preterite': ayer, anoche, la semana pasada, el año pasado, en 2010, una vez.

topics.title: The imperfect — what you used to do
topics.description: Talk about habits, ongoing scenes, and 'when I was a kid…'.

guide.intro: The imperfect (pretérito imperfecto) is the past for things without a clear end: routines, ongoing states, descriptions, ages, weather, and feelings in the past.

rows.source: hablar → hablaba, hablabas, hablaba, hablábamos, hablabais, hablaban
rows.translation: I used to speak / I was speaking

rows.source: comer → comía, comías, comía, comíamos, comíais, comían
rows.translation: I used to eat / I was eating

rows.source: vivir → vivía, vivías, vivía, vivíamos, vivíais, vivían
rows.translation: I used to live / I was living

sections.text: All -er and -ir verbs share one set of endings (-ía). That makes the imperfect easier than the preterite.

rows.source: ser → era, eras, era, éramos, erais, eran
rows.translation: I was, you were, he/she was…

rows.source: ir → iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, ibais, iban
rows.translation: I used to go / I was going

rows.source: ver → veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veíais, veían
rows.translation: I used to see / I was seeing

sections.text: Use the imperfect for: (a) habits — 'every Sunday we ate paella'; (b) ongoing background — 'it was raining'; (c) age, time, weather in the past — 'tenía diez años', 'eran las tres'; (d) feelings/states — 'estaba cansado'.
English clue words: 'used to', 'would (often)', 'was/were -ing'. If you can rewrite a sentence with one of those, you almost always want the imperfect.

topics.title: Preterite vs imperfect — the big choice
topics.description: When to use which past. The single most useful skill at A2.

guide.intro: Spanish forces a choice English doesn't: was the past action a finished event (preterite) or an ongoing scene/habit (imperfect)? Same English sentence often maps to either, depending on what you mean.

sections.text: Ask yourself: 'Could I add WHEN this happened (a specific time)?' If yes → preterite. 'Was this the background, what was going on, what used to happen?' → imperfect.

rows.translation: Yesterday I ate pizza. (one event, finished)

rows.source: De niño, comía pizza todos los viernes.
rows.translation: As a kid I used to eat pizza every Friday. (habit)
I was eating pizza when you called me. (ongoing + interrupting event)

sections.text: When something interrupts an ongoing scene, Spanish uses BOTH tenses in one sentence: the scene is imperfect, the interruption is preterite.

rows.source: Yo dormía cuando sonó el teléfono.
rows.translation: I was sleeping when the phone rang.

rows.source: Veíamos la tele cuando llegó mi padre.
rows.translation: We were watching TV when my father arrived.

rows.source: Preterite triggers: ayer, anoche, el lunes, una vez, de repente, en 2010.
Imperfect triggers: siempre, normalmente, todos los días, mientras, cuando era niño.

sections.text: Same verb, different meaning depending on tense: 'conocí a María' = I met María (for the first time); 'conocía a María' = I knew María (already).

guide.intro: Reflexive verbs end in -se in the dictionary (lavarse, ducharse, llamarse) and need a matching pronoun (me, te, se, nos, os, se) before a conjugated verb. They're routine in Spanish for things you do to yourself.
